Guard every consumer of PACKS against an empty list: the boot call switchPack(PACKS[0]) at main.js:264 (skip it when PACKS is empty), hud.setPacks (render a disabled placeholder option), and the COMPLETE handler's switchPack(PACKS[0]) at main.js:196. Additionally, add an r.ok / content-type check in loadPack (pack-loader.js) so a missing pack fails with a clear error instead of a JSON SyntaxError on SPA-fallback HTML. In the COMPLETE handler (main.js:199-200), if the refetched index does not contain packName (transient fetch failure), append packName to PACKS before hud.setPacks so the select always has a matching option.

summary: updateZoneLabels rebuilds the label DOM only when the band COUNT changes, so switching between two layouts with the same number of zones but different zone names shows the previous layout's letters.
scenario: Operator loads a pack whose active zones are B and C (2 bands), then switches to a pack whose zones are A and D (also 2 bands). `layer.childElementCount !== layout.zoneBands.length` is false, so the spans keep the text 'B'/'C' while positions/radii come from the new layout — the artwork is annotated with the wrong zones until a pack with a different zone count happens to be loaded.
fix_sketch: Key the rebuild on the names too, e.g. cache `layout.zoneBands.map(b => b.zone).join()` on the layer (dataset attribute) and rebuild when it differs.
reasoning: hud.js line 93 gates the label DOM rebuild solely on child count vs zoneBands.length; the zone letters are only written inside that branch, while the per-frame loop below updates positions/opacity from the new layout unconditionally. switchPack in main.js never clears hud.labelLayer, and manifest zones are derived per-pack from whichever zone letters appear in that session (viz-pack.js), so two packs with equal zone counts but different letters are realistic (live vs loadgen packs, or live-mode rosterLayout followed by a pack). A tmp-repro (tmp-repro/zone-label-stale.mjs) importing the real updateZoneLabels with a minimal DOM stub shows: pack1 (B,C) -> labels B,C; pack2 (A,D, same count) -> labels still B,C; only a 3-band layout triggers the rebuild. The claimed failure occurs exactly as described.
corrected_fix: Key the rebuild on zone names, not just count — e.g. compute `const key = layout.zoneBands.map(b => b.zone).join('|')` and rebuild when `layer.dataset.zones !== key` (then set `layer.dataset.zones = key`). Since updateZoneLabels runs every frame, keep the cached-key comparison rather than rebuilding unconditionally; alternatively, set each span's textContent from band.zone inside the existing forEach when it differs.

summary: The 'kayıt boş kaldı' (empty recording) message is overwritten within the same tick by the automatic switchPack, so the operator never learns why nothing new appeared.
scenario: A recording completes with zero participants (upstream quiet): COMPLETE arrives with packName null, handleLive sets stats to 'kayıt boş kaldı — akışta hiç olay yoktu' and immediately awaits switchPack(PACKS[0]), whose first action is hud.setStats('yükleniyor…') (main.js:95) followed by the pack's stats line. The explanation is visible for milliseconds; the operator just sees the old pack reload and may re-record blindly instead of checking the upstream feed.
fix_sketch: Show the empty-recording notice in the rec button / a dedicated toast that switchPack does not touch, or pass an optional statsSuffix through switchPack so the message survives the reload.
reasoning: The failure occurs exactly as described, and is in fact slightly worse than claimed. Server (src/server.js:98-106): an empty session (participants === 0) skips packing and broadcasts {kind:'state', state:'COMPLETE', packName:null}. Client (viz/src/main.js:191-198): handleLive calls stopLiveUi(null), which sets live=null, so the guard `if (live) return` in switchPack (line 93) does not block; line 195 sets stats to 'kayıt boş kaldı — akışta hiç olay yoktu' via hud.setStats (a synchronous textContent write, hud.js:66), and line 196's `await switchPack(PACKS[0])` synchronously executes switchPack's first statement hud.setStats('yükleniyor…') (line 95) before its first await. Both DOM writes happen in the same JS task, and browsers only paint between tasks, so the empty-recording message is never painted at all — not even for milliseconds. After the pack loads, lines 111-114 overwrite stats again with the pack summary (or 'paket yüklenemedi' on failure). PACKS is effectively never empty (FALLBACK_PACKS, lines 12/17-18), so the overwrite path always runs. summary: When the live disc is built from the 12000-event fallback roster (no upstream snapshot yet), only 64 spare lanes absorb every participant not heard in the first ~0.4s; the 65th+ latecomer gets laneOf() === null and all their grains are silently dropped from the live artwork for the whole session.

Additionally, stop ignoring the authoritative roster: mark the disc as fallback-built and, when a 'kind:"roster"' message arrives for a fallback disc, rebuild layout+disc and re-append retained events (keep a session-scoped array of applied events in live mode to make the rebuild lossless). summary: The Space shortcut is only intercepted in pack mode, so during a live take Space (or Enter) activates the still-focused KAYIT button and stops the 90s recording.

reasoning: Code reading confirms every link in the chain. (1) main.js:83-90: the window keydown handler calls e.preventDefault() for Space only inside `if (e.key === ' ' && current)`, and startRecording() (main.js:126) sets `current = null` before live mode begins, so Space's default action is never suppressed during a take; Enter is never handled in any mode. (2) hud.js:48 wires `$('rec').onclick = onRecord` with no blur() anywhere, and setLiveMode(true) (hud.js:79-83) disables play/restart/scrub/speed/final/export/pack but deliberately leaves #rec enabled as the stop button. The abort path still finalizes and auto-packs data captured so far (server.js:95-106), so the loss is the remainder of the unrepeatable 90s window, not the whole session. The trigger is realistic: Space is the replay-mode play/pause habit key and nothing moves focus off #rec after the mouse click. Pack mode is protected for Space (preventDefault runs before the default action), so the claimed live/pack asymmetry is genuine.
corrected_fix: In hud.js, blur transport buttons on click so keyboard focus never lingers on them — e.g. wrap the button handlers: `$('rec').onclick = (e) => { e.currentTarget.blur(); onRecord(); };` (and similarly for the other buttons). This fixes both the Space and the Enter activation paths. The alternative sketch — unconditionally preventDefault-ing Space in the main.js keydown handler regardless of `current` — closes only the Space path and leaves Enter-on-focused-button live, so the blur approach is the complete remedy (optionally combined with the unconditional Space preventDefault so Space still means play/pause only).

summary: index.json is updated with an unlocked, non-atomic read-modify-write (readFileSync ... writeFileSync), so concurrent packers in different processes (server auto-pack + CLI pack) silently lose entries, and a torn read of a mid-write file hits the catch and resets the index to just the new pack, discarding the whole history.
scenario: Server autopack fires at session completion while the operator CLI-packs an older session into the same packs dir: both read the index before either writes, last write wins and one pack vanishes from the viewer's pack list; worse, if one reads while the other is mid-writeFileSync (O_TRUNC then write), JSON.parse fails and the catch rebuilds index as {packs:[entry]} — every previously packed session disappears from discovery until manually re-packed. Probability per collision is low (microsecond window) but the loss is silent and permanent.
fix_sketch: Rebuild index.packs by scanning dirname(outDir) for subdirectories containing manifest.json instead of trusting the previous file contents, and write atomically (writeFileSync to index.json.tmp + renameSync). Either change alone removes the permanent-loss mode; both together remove torn reads too.
repro_evidence: tmp-repro/race-worker.js run as two concurrent processes packing 300 uniquely-named tiny sessions each into a shared dir: final out-race/packs/index.json held 71 of 600 entries (529 silently lost).
reasoning: Read src/viz-pack.js lines 127-135: index.json is updated with an unlocked read-modify-write (readFileSync -> mutate -> writeFileSync, no tmp+rename), and the catch on line 129 — intended for the first-pack ENOENT case — also swallows JSON.parse failures from reading a file mid-writeFileSync (O_TRUNC then write), resetting index to { packs: [] } so line 135 rewrites it with only the new entry. The concurrent-process scenario is real: src/server.js:100-102 auto-packs into viz/public/packs/ inside the server process on session completion, while src/viz-pack.js:140-145 is a standalone CLI packing into the same dir, and viz/src/main.js:15 discovers packs solely via /packs/index.json, so a lost entry hides the pack from the viewer. Ran a tmp-repro (tmp-repro/race-worker.js): two concurrent processes each packing 300 uniquely-named tiny sessions into a shared packs dir left only 9 of 600 entries in index.json while all 600 pack directories existed on disk — proving both last-write-wins lost updates and the torn-read history-wipe. Loss is silent (no error) and nothing rebuilds the index; pack data survives so entries are recoverable by re-packing, matching the claim's own scoping. Severity minor is fair: microsecond-scale collision window, few sessions per real night, and index entries are rebuildable — but the failure genuinely occurs.
corrected_fix: In packSession (src/viz-pack.js:126-135), stop trusting the previous index.json contents: rebuild index.packs by scanning dirname(outDir) for subdirectories containing a manifest.json (reading each manifest for sessionId/laneCount/eventCount/strokeCount, or keeping a per-pack entry.json), then write atomically via writeFileSync(indexPath + '.tmp', json) followed by renameSync to index.json. The scan makes the index self-healing regardless of interleaving; the atomic rename ensures readers never see a truncated/partial file. Either change alone removes the permanent-loss mode; both together also eliminate torn reads.

summary: The reconnect backoff sleep (`await new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, delay))`) ignores the abort signal, so an abort during an upstream outage is only honored after the sleep expires — up to maxRetryDelayMs (4s with shipped defaults) of stop latency.
scenario: Upstream is flapping mid-recording and liveSource is inside its backed-off sleep (delay has climbed to 4000ms). The operator hits Stop on the panel (/api/stop -> controller.abort()) — or the durationMs+5000 killer fires. Nothing wakes the sleep; the source keeps 'recording' state for up to 4 more seconds until the timer elapses and the next fetch rejects on the aborted signal. The panel appears unresponsive to Stop, and the wall-clock killer's cutoff drifts by up to 4s.
repro_evidence: Inline node repro: liveSource({url:'http://127.0.0.1:1/', signal, retryDelayMs:3000}); aborted the controller 100ms into the backoff sleep; the generator only ended after 3001ms ('abort at +100ms ... source actually ended after 3001 ms').
fix_sketch: Make the sleep abort-aware: `await new Promise((r) => { const t = setTimeout(r, delay); signal?.addEventListener('abort', () => { clearTimeout(t); r(); }, { once: true }); })` (or setTimeout from node:timers/promises with { signal } and a caught AbortError), then check `signal?.aborted` and return before the next fetch.
reasoning: Line 36 of src/sources/live-source.js is a bare `await new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, delay))` with no abort listener; only the setTimeout can resolve it. During a backoff sleep no fetch is in flight, so controller.abort() has nothing to cancel and nothing wakes the generator until the sleep expires (delay caps at maxRetryDelayMs=4000 with shipped defaults — server.js line 201 passes no overrides). The consequence chain checks out in the callers: recorder.js consumes the source via `for await` (line 38) and its stopAfterMs check (line 40) only runs between yields, so it cannot fire while the source sleeps; server.js /api/stop (line 119) merely calls controller.abort() and phase stays 'RECORDING' until the record promise settles, and the durationMs+5000 killer (line 91) has the same latency, drifting its cutoff by the residual sleep. Repro in tmp-repro/abort-backoff-repro.mjs (unreachable port, retryDelayMs=3000, abort at +102ms) showed the generator ending at +3012ms — the full sleep elapsed before the abort was honored. Blast radius is bounded: after the sleep, the next fetch rejects immediately on the aborted signal and the generator returns cleanly, so the recorder finalizes the session normally; the impact is purely up-to-~4s stop latency and killer-cutoff drift, matching the claimed 'minor' severity.
corrected_fix: Make the backoff sleep abort-aware, preferring the variant that cleans up after itself: `import { setTimeout as sleep } from 'node:timers/promises';` then `try { await sleep(delay, undefined, { signal }); } catch { return; }` (an AbortError here means stop was requested). This also removes its abort listener when the timer expires normally. The claim's inline-addEventListener variant works but leaks one listener per retry iteration on the shared signal (`{ once: true }` only removes it when abort actually fires), which can accumulate and trigger MaxListenersExceededWarning during a long flapping outage — if using that form, also removeEventListener when the timeout fires. Either way, check `signal?.aborted` and return before the next fetch.
